How it works Shading Playground Patterns

A single-file field guide · real-time graphics

Ray Marching

A family of rendering techniques that finds surfaces by walking a ray through a field of distance — one exact, safe step at a time. No meshes, no ray tracing: just a function that answers how far, and the patience to keep walking.

WebGL · GLSL Signed distance fields 60 fps in your browser
Open the playground ↓ How it works

Every demo on this page is computed live on your GPU. No videos, no pre-rendered frames — it's really marching right now.

live · ray-marched in your browser move to steer the camera
01 · The big idea

No triangles. Just a distance.

Classic rendering gives the GPU a mesh — millions of little triangles it tests against. Ray marching inverts the problem: describe the whole scene as a signed distance field, a function f(p) that tells you, for any point p, how far you are from the nearest surface (positive outside, negative inside). The surface lives wherever f(p) = 0.

core_walk.glsl 
// One ray per pixel: build a camera, then walk it to the surface
vec3 ro = vec3(0.0, 0.6, 3.0);  // camera position
vec3 ta = vec3(0.0, 0.3, 0.0);  // where we're aiming
vec3 fw = normalize(ta - ro);
vec3 rt = normalize(cross(fw, vec3(0.0,1.0,0.0)));
vec3 up = cross(rt, fw);
vec3 rd = normalize(uv.x * rt + uv.y * up + 1.7 * fw);

float t = 0.0;
for (int i = 0; i < 128; i++) {
    vec3  p = ro + rd * t;   // probe point along the ray
    float d = sceneSDF(p); // signed distance to the surface

    if (d < 0.001) break;  // hit — p is on the surface
    t += d;               // exact step: can never skip the surface
}
02 · The walk

Four moves, repeated a hundred times

The whole trick fits in a dozen lines. Each of these four moves happens per pixel, per frame — hundreds of millions of times a second on your GPU.

1

Aim a ray

Every pixel spawns a ray from the camera. This part is the classic per-pixel camera — nothing special. The magic starts after this line.

2

Query the field

Evaluate f(p) at the probe point. A positive number means “you're outside, this far” — and it's an exact lower bound, not an estimate.

3

Step — safely

Advance the ray by exactly d. Because d is a true distance, the new point can never cross the surface. No missed hits, no tunnelling, ever.

4

Converge & shade

Repeat until d ≈ 0. Then estimate a normal from the field, march shadows toward the light, light the point, and write the pixel.

distance_fields.glsl 
// A signed distance field (SDF): the entire "mesh" is this function.
// f(p) > 0 → outside · f(p) < 0 → inside · f(p) = 0 → the surface

float sdSphere(vec3 p, float r) { return length(p) - r; }

float sdBox(vec3 p, vec3 b) {
    vec3 q = abs(p) - b;
    return length(max(q, 0.0)) + min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0.0);
}

// Boolean composition — this is how you model with math
float unionSDF(float a, float b)       { return min(a, b); }
float intersectSDF(float a, float b) { return max(a, b); }

// Smooth union — the operator behind every metaball effect
float smin(float a, float b, float k) {
    float h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 * (b - a) / k, 0.0, 1.0);
    return mix(b, a, h) - k * h * (1.0 - h);
}
Why it matters

A single SDF function can describe a 100-million-polygon scene in a few hundred bytes. That's why ray marching powers procedural worlds on Shadertoy, metaball and goo effects in games, and even accelerated path tracing — the whole scene is just math you can differentiate.

03 · From a hit to a pixel

A surface with no data is still shadeable

When the walk converges you hold a bare point — no mesh, no normals, no UVs. The beautiful part: the SDF gives you everything back, for free. Differentiate it for normals, re-march it for shadows, and light it like anything.

Normal estimation

Normals without meshes

Sample the SDF on a tiny tetrahedron around the hit and normalize the result. A four-call gradient that's smooth to the last pixel — no faceting, no stored data.

Lighting model

Light that reads the field

Diffuse, bounce light and a fresnel rim all come straight from the normal and the ray direction. Materials become palette choices, not texture files.

Soft shadows

March toward the light

Fire a second ray at the light and accumulate how open the path is. The same SDF gives you penumbra softness instead of hard, binary cut-offs.

normals_lighting.glsl 
// No stored normals: estimate them from the SDF with a tetrahedron
vec3 calcNormal(vec3 p) {
    const vec2 e = vec2(0.001, 0.0);
    return normalize(vec3(
        sd(p + e.xyy) - sd(p - e.xyy),
        sd(p + e.yxy) - sd(p - e.yxy),
        sd(p + e.yyx) - sd(p - e.yyx)));
}

vec3 shade(vec3 p, vec3 n, vec3 rd) {
    vec3  lig = normalize(vec3(0.7, 0.9, -0.4));
    float dif = clamp(dot(n, lig), 0.0, 1.0);
    float bac = clamp(dot(n, -lig), 0.0, 1.0);
    float fre = pow(clamp(1.0 + dot(n, rd), 0.0, 1.0), 3.0);
    vec3  alb = vec3(0.9, 0.45, 0.3);

    return alb * (0.6 * dif + 0.25 * bac + 0.35)     // diffuse · bounce · ambient
         + vec3(1.0)  * fre * 0.25                    // fresnel rim
         + vec3(1.0,0.9,0.8) * pow(dif, 64.0);        // specular
}
The tetrahedron trick: three axis-aligned sample pairs give a full 3D gradient in 6 evaluations, cheaper and smoother than 8.
soft_shadow.glsl 
// March a second ray toward the light; never sample the SDF directly
float softShadow(vec3 ro, vec3 rd) {
    float res = 1.0;
    float t   = 0.02;
    for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
        float h = sd(ro + rd * t);
        res = min(res, 10.0 * h / t);  // h / t → penumbra softness
        t  += clamp(h, 0.02, 0.35);
        if (res < 0.004 || t > 12.0) break;
    }
    return clamp(res, 0.0, 1.0);
}
Why it's soft: multiplying distance by 1/t turns “how close is an occluder” into “how much light gets through”. It's the same safe-stepping rule, just aimed at the sun.

A self-contained, single-file webpage (no external libraries, fonts, or images — everything inline) with a professional dark theme by default and a light theme toggle.

**Structure:**
- **Sticky topbar** — wordmark logo, section nav, and a sun/moon theme toggle (persisted via `localStorage`, no flash on reload).
- **Full-viewport hero** — live WebGL ray-marched scene (sphere + cube + octahedron over a noisy floor) with mouse-look camera, headline, and quick-nav chips.

- **03 · Shading** — cards for normal estimation / lighting / soft shadows, with two more copyable GLSL blocks (tetrahedron normals, soft-shadow march) and captions explaining the math.

- **05 · Beyond 3D** — four animated 2D GLSL tiles (fbm ridges, voronoi, moiré, wave interference) sharing the same pipeline.

**Technical details:**
- All five WebGL programs (hero, playground, 4 tiles) share one lightweight boilerplate; shader compile errors degrade gracefully with a "WebGL unavailable" notice instead of breaking the page.
- Hand-tokenized GLSL code blocks with a Copy button (clipboard API + fallback).
- Responsive down to mobile (grids collapse, tiles stack), `prefers-reduced-motion` support, scroll-reveal animations, scanline/grid ambience, and full light-theme token overrides (code blocks stay dark in both themes for readability).

Query the field

// A signed distance field (SDF): the entire "mesh" is this function.
// f(p) > 0 → outside · f(p) < 0 → inside · f(p) = 0 → the surface

float sdSphere(vec3 p, float r) { return length(p) - r; }

float sdBox(vec3 p, vec3 b) {
    vec3 q = abs(p) - b;
    return length(max(q, 0.0)) + min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0.0);
}

// Boolean composition — this is how you model with math
float unionSDF(float a, float b)       { return min(a, b); }
float intersectSDF(float a, float b) { return max(a, b); }

// Smooth union — the operator behind every metaball effect
float smin(float a, float b, float k) {
    float h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 * (b - a) / k, 0.0, 1.0);

A single SDF function can describe a 100-million-polygon scene in a few hundred bytes. That's why ray marching powers procedural worlds on Shadertoy, metaball and goo effects in games, and even accelerated path tracing — the whole scene is just math you can differentiate.

03 · From a hit to a pixel

A surface with no data is still shadeable

When the walk converges you hold a bare point — no mesh, no normals, no UVs. The beautiful part: the SDF gives you everything back, for free. Differentiate it for normals, re-march it for shadows, and light it like anything.

Normal estimation

Normals without meshes

Sample the SDF on a tiny tetrahedron around the hit and normalize the result. A four-call gradient that's smooth to the last pixel — no faceting, no stored data.

Lighting model

Light that reads the field

Diffuse, bounce light and a fresnel rim all come straight from the normal and the ray direction. Materials become palette choices, not texture files.

Fire a second ray at the light and accumulate how open the path is. The same SDF gives you penumbra softness instead of hard, binary cut-offs.

normals_lighting.glsl 
// No stored normals: estimate them from the SDF with a tetrahedron
vec3 calcNormal(vec3 p) {
    const vec2 e = vec2(0.001, 0.0);
    return normalize(vec3(
        sd(p + e.xyy) - sd(p - e.xyy),
        sd(p + e.yxy) - sd(p - e.yxy),
        sd(p + e.yyx) - sd(p - e.yyx)));
}

vec3 shade(vec3 p, vec3 n, vec3 rd) {
    vec3  lig = normalize(vec3(0.7, 0.9, -0.4));
    float dif = clamp(dot(n, lig), 0.0, 1.0);
    float bac = clamp(dot(n, -lig), 0.0, 1.0);
    float fre = pow(clamp(1.0 + dot(n, rd), 0.0, 1.0), 3.0);
    vec3  alb = vec3(0.9, 0.45, 0.3);

    return alb * (0.6 * dif + 0.25 * bac + 0.35)     // diffuse · bounce · ambient
         + vec3(1.0)  * fre * 0.25                    // fresnel rim
         + vec3(1.0,0.9,0.8) * pow(dif, 64.0);        // specular
}

soft_shadow.glsl 
// March a second ray toward the light; never sample the SDF directly
float softShadow(vec3 ro, vec3 rd) {
    float res = 1.0;
    float t   = 0.02;
    for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
        float h = sd(ro + rd * t);
        res = min(res, 10.0 * h / t);  // h / t → penumbra softness
        t  += clamp(h, 0.02, 0.35);
        if (res < 0.004 || t > 12.0) break;
    }
    return clamp(res, 0.0, 1.0);
}
Why it's soft: multiplying distance by 1/t turns “how close is an occluder” into “how much light gets through”. It's the same safe-stepping rule, just aimed at the sun.
